2019 marks the 400th anniversary of the longest-running legislature in the Americas: the Virginia Assembly. Trump’s speech before the General Assembly at Williamsburg marks the first time a sitting US president has addressed the Assembly, and Trump’s speech honored not only the 400 years of continual governance, but the political philosophy developed and executed largely by Virginians early in United States history, and the character and legacy which it has left the country as a whole.

Trump went as far back as to pay respect to the English legal traditions we inherited by having a former legal expert of the British government lawyer present at the ceremony, and the political message of Trump’s speech seems to be a modern interpretation of those legal traditions as our founders understood them. The language was very Jeffersonian from the outset: Trump celebrated Virginia’s role in the “righteous cause of self-government,” and welcomed leaders from “federal, state, local, and tribal” positions, as if to re-emphasize in even greater detail the hierarchy of powers set up in the Jeffersonian system. Jefferson himself both feared empire and stressed the decentralized and separate spheres of political power, but was also an imperialist in the sense that he wanted his particular brand of confederated republics to occupy the entire North American continent, and that is pretty much exactly what unfolded until the admissions of Alaska and Hawaii.

Anyway, the entire speech is filled with historic symbolism and deserves more analysis. Together with his speech in Poland and a few others, this one is bound to be remembered by presidential historians.
